newsitem.title: USA: Trial to start in 1993 World Trade Center bombing.
newsitem.headline: Trial to start in 1993 World Trade Center bombing.

text.p: Jury selection is set to start on Tuesday for the trial of Ramzi Ahmed Yousef, the alleged mastermind of the 1993 World Trade Centre bombing, and his co-defendant, Eyad Ismoil, a court official said.
Yousef and Ismoil are accused of planting a 1,200-pound (544 kilogram) fertiliser bomb that killed six people, injured more than 1,000 and caused millions of dollars in damage.

Yousef was indicted in 1993 on charges of taking part in the bombing, along with four others, who were convicted in 1994. The other defendants were each sentenced to more than 200 years in prison for their roles in the devastating explosion.
Ismoil, a Jordanian, is accused of driving the van that carried the bomb into the basement garage of the Trade Centre complex.
Yousef holds an Iraqi passport but claims Pakistani and Palestinian ancestry. He said in a statement after his capture that he was an electronics engineer and explosives expert.
He was one of the world's most wanted fugitives until his arrest in February 1995 in Pakistan.
Prosecutors say Yousef fled the country on a plane to Karachi, Pakistan, just hours after the explosion.

A jury pool of 75 prospects will be called daily to the courtroom of U.S. District Judge Kevin Duffy until a 12-member panel and six alternates are sworn to hear the testimony. Jury selection is expected to take two to three weeks.
In 1996 Yousef and two other radical Moslems were convicted of planning to bomb 12 U.S. passenger jets to punish the United States for its support of Israel.
In that plot, Yousef was convicted of being the architect of a scheme to murder about 4,000 passengers over a 48-hour period as they returned on U.S. airliners from the East Asia.

He was also convicted of placing a bomb on a Philippine Airlines flight from Manila to Tokyo in 1994 as a trial run. The bomb exploded under the seat of a Japanese passenger, killing him and injuring 10 other people.
At Yousef's trial last year, he defended himself, but he has decided this time to be represented by court-appointed lawyer Roy Kulcsar, his legal adviser at the earlier trial.
He has not yet been sentenced for the airline plot.
